content: The analysis included 26 studies, 18 of which involved surgical interventions and 8 that did not. All studies were observational, raising concerns about selection bias. Patients selected for surgery may have had either more favorable or less favorable prognostic factors, and the duration of treatment varied significantly between surgical and non-surgical groups. This suggests that differences in medical regimens could influence outcomes, although these and other potential confounders were accounted for in adjusted analyses. Regarding consistency, the estimated I-squared values showed similar results for treatment success versus failure or relapse (+/death). However, the odds ratio (OR) for success increased when individuals lost to follow-up were included in the analysis. No indirectness was expected, as all patients were treated for multidrug-resistant (MDR) or extensively drug-resistant (XDR) tuberculosis (TB). The outcomes of success, failure, relapse, and death were deemed critical by the Guideline Development Group, although loss to follow-up was not a specified outcome but remains relevant. The precision of the effect estimates was assessed using 95% confidence limits, with pooled success proportions ranging from 51% to 79% across different studies. Adjusted effect estimates were calculated using one-to-one propensity score matching between surgical and non-surgical patients. The interest in reducing the duration of MDR-TB treatment has led to initiatives exploring shorter regimens under both programmatic and trial conditions. Recent studies from Bangladesh, Cameroon, and Niger have shown higher treatment success rates with 12-month or shorter regimens compared to longer conventional regimens, provided specific inclusion criteria were met. However, due to limited experience with these shorter regimens, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended their use only within operational research settings and under close monitoring for safety and effectiveness. Shorter MDR-TB regimens have demonstrated relapse-free cure rates exceeding 85% among selected patients, with fewer adverse events compared to longer regimens. Gatifloxacin, a key drug in shorter regimens, was previously associated with dysglycemia in elderly patients but has since been shown to be safe in TB treatment. The benefits of its use outweigh the risks, especially given the severity of MDR-TB. Shorter regimens exclude drugs commonly associated with severe adverse events, such as cycloserine and linezolid. The overall certainty of evidence for shorter regimens is very low, as it is based on observational studies. Randomized controlled trial (RCT) data are not expected until after 2017. Despite this, the WHO Guideline Development Group recommends shorter regimens for patients with rifampicin-resistant or MDR-TB who have not been previously treated with second-line drugs and are unlikely to have resistance to fluoroquinolones or second-line injectable agents. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low certainty in the evidence. Patients with additional resistance to pyrazinamide or fluoroquinolones had lower treatment success rates, although these rates still exceeded those of patients on individualized, longer regimens. Children and people living with HIV should be considered for shorter regimens under the same criteria as adults. However, pregnant women and patients with extrapulmonary TB were excluded from studies, and no recommendations can be made for these groups at this time. Reliable and rapid diagnostic tests are essential to identify eligible patients and guide treatment modifications. Monitoring and evaluation should follow established clinical and laboratory testing schedules, with active drug-safety monitoring and management (aDSM) frameworks in place. Longer, individualized regimens remain necessary for patients ineligible for shorter regimens due to additional drug resistance, extrapulmonary disease, or other contraindications. These regimens have been used successfully for decades and are supported by improved availability and reduced costs of core second-line drugs. However, challenges remain in procuring certain medications, such as bedaquiline and delamanid, which are still expensive.
